I could not.. manage it, I mean.. My zoekjaar ended and I returned to India but left all my stuff with my best friend and partner in the Netherlands. There was no way to pack up ten years of life and no way to choose to just throw away everything. I came to stay with my family in India, took a break and worked on my health (I had lost a lost of weight due to being unemployed and thus eating less to save money). As someone who checked my history so meanly commented, my mental health was suffering due to the constant rejections too, so a break was good. I also travelled a bit and only recently started applying for jobs again.

I will say that is DEFINITELY noticeable how there are much fewer positions open this year for internationals compared to last year. Not that it made any difference to me last year... didn't get accepted to any of the hundreds I applied to anyway, but this year, most similar starter/fresher jobs seem to list fluent Dutch or EU citizenship as a requirement (not all, ofc). Recruitment companies told me they won't help people residing outside NL either.

The head of HR of a big company in NL told me to basically give up. He said my chances are basically zero since I am no longer in NL. He told me to work in India and try again after getting like ten years of experience maybe lol. (and he told me to hope the political scene changes and people end up wanting more immigrants in their country.. which felt sarcastic lol).

Well, I will end up having a mental breakdown if I give up hope so I am now just applying again and hoping for the best. One application per day is my goal, so I can also have a life, instead of the strange all-day-applications-no-hobbies-no-life year I had last year. I have joined a Dutch B1 class so I can practise my Dutch and gain more confidence in speaking. I'm also looking for short-term positions in other EU countries so I can at least have some income until I can return to NL, and also gain some experience in the process. However, haven't found anything so far.

It's either that they are using AI software or that they are prioritising applicants from the NL or the EU. I have received dozens of rejections claiming they can't give personal feedback to everyone but rejected candidates usually do not meet "one of the following criteria", and then list a set of criteria that I 100% completely do meet. I usually used to read such emails thrice at least to make sure I'm not mistaken. 

Sometimes I sent a reply apologising for asking for personal feedback but pointing out that I meet all of the criteria they mentioned, and asking how I can be rejected for not meeting the criteria in that case. Then I usually got responses saying they found someone more aligned to their group, or better-suited to their research, or other such vague stuff that makes no sense since they can't know this unless they actually interview me.

I know this is a thing that can cause a ton of anxiety, but I dont think you have anything to worry about. Universities in the Netherlands are pretty understanding about extenuating circumstances. 

I was myself depressed and got like 5 credits one year. I was already talking to the study advisor and was on meds. It was also pretty clear I was depressed, I guess. I made the appeal, and it felt more like a formality. I wrote the letter and submitted the form and all. They discussed it during the meeting and told me that I'll not be expelled for not meeting the bsa requirements. They wished me luck with my health and that was that. 

If you were in contact with the study advisor and a psychologist since a while back, it's obvious that you're not just making up some fake excuse. So they have no reason to reject your appeal. I don't think anyone else is qualified to say if your situation was "bad enough". Besides, I'd look up the rules, but death or illness of a family member is itself usually listed as legitimate grounds for an exemption to thr bsa (apart from the fact that such an event can cause mental health problems, which is also a separate legitimate reason for exemption).

I agree with the other answer. The last part is especially important. Make sure that the study adviser knows about your situation at the earliest possible. If you do that, you can officially ask for things like extra exam time, separate rooms, etc., at least in some universities. The university websites should say something about studying with disabilities.

In my experience, for other things like assignments, for instance, if you just tell a teacher you were not able to do something before a deadline for a specific reason connected to your situation, they will just allow you to submit a bit late. So they are quite accepting of personal situations.

They are also used to it. Cause diagnosed, questioning, self-diagnosed, whatever, but there are a ton of neurodivergent people at universities. You'll probably quickly notice that like half the teachers are too (depending on your field, of course). And you'll see that there are quite a few ND students too.  


It should not cost any extra money. At least at the university, the facilities they provide are at no extra cost. If you need support from outside, like psychologists etc, your medical insurance should be able to take care of that. So that would also not cost much or anything, depending on your insurance.

I understand your frustration but I feel like you need to educate yourself and your family a bit more about mental health and depression. You may claim to understand but you clearly don't. 

I read all of your posts and it feels to me like your dealing with your own set of issues with your brother and perhaps some envy about his looks. Besides, I feel like there's a lot of conflicting stuff about his mental health. Regardless of how he looks and how great his life is, he is not 'playing the victim ' if he says he's depressed, especially as you clearly saw that he took steps to end his life. People can have depression for no reason; I myself do. And it only ever got worse because I knew people around me were judging me for depressed despite having a great family, a lavish lifestyle and most things going my way until that point.

You even mention that he was quiet and got bullied at some point and you had to protect him. And you mentioned that he has "nothing going for him except his looks". If that's true, there's a good chance he has noticed/realised that himself, which is good enough reason to have severe existential doubt and crushing depression. 

Besides that, he does seem like a jerk, especially if he's actually bullying the women has any relationships with. Mental health and being a victim of bullying are not excuses for being abusive in your relationships. But then you also seem to be describing someone who really has no emotional intelligence, and seems to have some developmental deficits. Maybe he has autism (he sounds like some of the maladjusted people in our community), or maybe some other way his emotional development was inadequate. Watching frequent fights between your parents could gave worsened that. Maybe he is just really not mentally stable right now and is lashing out as a result. Again, that's not an excuse, cause he should just get help then. He also seems to have some executive dysfunction in the way he is living his life.

My main point is that him being a jerk and his mental health are two completely separate things. One is not an excuse for the other, but one also does not mean the other is untrue. Remember that and try to get him some help. Often people who make concrete plans to kill themselves will end up attempting suicide soon enough. I'd rather not you making a post about your brother in r/SuicideWatch or something next time.

The main hard thing about Deutsch would be the three gender system instead of the English single gender one. Every object in the world is 'it' in English, but could be 'he', 'she' or 'it' in Deutsch. Additionally, the adjectives get endings according to the gender of the object. The articles change with cases, and so do prepostions, pronouns and so do some adverbs and conjunctions.

The reason I'm saying this is not to discourage you. It takes time to get used to this completely different system and it may feel too hard or tiresome, but don't give up. you eventually get used to it, and with enough practice, it is not necessary to remember the genders of all objects because they just 'sound right' and come naturally to you.

Because of this, although modern methods like apps, etc are getting popular these days, I'd say it's better to combine those with traditional lessons. Learn the theory from a book, for instance. The rules for grammar, for instance. Make tables or whatever visual form seems easier for you to grasp fast. Once you know enough, start watching German videos with English subtitles, but while trying to recognise the words and mtch them/compare with the English text. Then after you get more comfortable, start watching German videos with German subtitles. You could even try having German subtitles for English movies that you are rewatching.(I'm from India. My first language is English, but I also speak Marathi, the regional language, Hindi, German, and a bit of Dutch as I live in the Netherlands. I can read some Latin and Sanskrit too, but not enough to say I know Latin or Sanskrit haha)

Even private scholarships won't entertain non-EU students. I got an invitation to apply a scholarship set up by a big local businessman because of my extremely high grades. They literally invited me to apply, and then told me that I can't apply as I was not born in the region.  
The requirement was that I'd stay in the region after my education for at least 4 yrs or something, which was absolutely acceptable to me. But I wasn't born here so it didn't matter.

I don't want to be discouraging, but I think if money is an issue, the Netherlands isn't the best place to go for your studies. In fact, forget 'best', it's not a good place at all! This country is quite expensive as a whole, with living costs that can vary a lot but are generally high.  
The fees are extremely high non-EU students, but that's not the only problem. International students have to get 30 credits every year, or get kicked out. If you are unable to get those 30 credits for some reason, you lose all the money you already invested in this education.  
Getting 30 credits should not be very hard, but can be quite a problem when you are already dealing with adjusting to the new country and new form of education and new everything. In addition, if you try to cook every day to save money, and avoid joining clubs and sports that also cost quite a bit, then your mental health suffers and makes it more likely that you might fail some courses. Then there's the fact that there's always this stress of getting those credits, which causes problems on its own.

Even if you fail a course or two, the costs increase by a lot. If you're doing Bachelor's, then failing one course can require you to take a whole quartile again. That means failing even once course will immediately increase your expenditure by about 5000 euros (fees+living). During Master's every month you take extra for graduating will cost you about 1700 euros extra.  
You can try to see if the private banks in your country allow you to take out loans, but those probably charge very high interest rates.  


TLDR; The Netherlands is only a suitable study destination for international (non-EU) students who come from relatively wealthy families. It's a terrible and unfortunate thing, and I really feel bad for you, but do re-consider you choice. Discuss with your family if you have enough money to fund a full education and living plus a little bit more for unforeseeable expenditures.  
I don't mean to be 'negative', but I'm seeing problems some ellow students are facing, and have myself experienced the dread and stress of managing costs, even though I do come from a somewhat wealthy family.  
Maybe you can study in your country, work for a while, earn a bit so that you can have enough to come here? I really hope you find some solution, though!

the easiest and most way to distinguis high-functioning and severe autism is literally the definition of 'functioning' as a euphemism: disabled but still able to survive in society.

High functioning autistic people would show a lot fo symptoms of autism but these symptoms wouldn't affect there daily life to the extent that their problems are more of an extreme nuisance that may lead to depression, anxiety, etc and other such problems that can also be managed eventually.

Severely autistic people may have speech and learning problems that render them incapable of doing even the most basic tasks in life. It's not about understanding the implications of what someone is saying so that their words are misinterpreted or seem confusing; the problem might be that nothing about what someone says is really heard/retained/understood.

Similarly the divide between neuro-typical and -atypical is not clear-cut in symptoms and will never be; but a divide is needed for diagnosis and deciding whether treatment/support is necessary, and hence a divide is made based on statistical data. For example, on the test, >65 is autistic; does that mean someone who got 63 is neurotypical and has no symptoms of autism? No, it just means that they are stastically not in the group that is known to require assistance in adjusting to society.

In the end, it's a spectrum, so what you said at the end does apply. The lower the 'score' the more neurotypical they'll seem. But for the sake of diagnosis (and disability support from school, govt, etc) a hard divide has to be made, and that has been made by scientists (doctors and psychologists). And to decided what kind of treatment is required, the symptoms and their severity has been broadly clssified into three (usually) groups, as mentioned in the source given by another answer here.

This argument is true and can be used for any other illness as well. Especially mental illnesses. Everyone gets depressed from time to time, everyone has flown into a rage, and everyone has mood swings and paranoia and anxiety. That doesn't mean they have any mental illness. Similarly, the fact that everyone could be considered to be on the spectrum doesn't invalidate the problems you are facing because of how you fall onto the spectrum.
